opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually one of the more underappreciated consequences of this whole line of work. When we started building systems like the AI Scientist, the immediate reaction from a lot of people was, "Great, now we'll be flooded with papers." And that's true. The cost of producing something that *looks* like a paper, with an idea, some experiments, plots, and a write-up, is collapsing toward almost nothing. But the cost of verifying whether that paper is actually correct, novel, and meaningful hasn't collapsed at all. That asymmetry is the core of it.

Historically, writing a paper was expensive. It took months of a PhD student's life, so there was a natural filter on volume, and peer review could sort of keep up, even if it was already creaking at venues like NeurIPS. Once generation becomes cheap, the bottleneck moves entirely to evaluation. Science doesn't just produce artifacts; it produces *trusted* knowledge, and review is where that trust gets manufactured.

There's also a more subtle point. These systems are optimizers, and if you optimize against any proxy, you'll find its weaknesses. If the proxy is "get past a reviewer," or even "get past an automated reviewer," you'll eventually get papers that are very good at looking like good papers. We saw small versions of this ourselves. The system would sometimes frame a modest result in a very convincing way, or an experiment would have a subtle bug that made the numbers look better than they were. A human scientist does that occasionally; an automated one can do it at scale.

So I think review has to become more rigorous and, in some ways, more mechanistic. Things like checking that code actually reproduces the reported numbers, auditing experimental setups, looking at whether baselines are tuned fairly. Some of that can and probably should be automated too. We built an automated reviewer partly for that reason, because you need evaluation to scale with generation. But I don't think you can fully close the loop with machines alone yet. You still need humans asking, "Is this interesting? Does this matter? Does it change how we think about the problem?" That judgment about significance is the part that's hardest to automate, and it's exactly the part that becomes most valuable when everything else gets cheap.

And honestly, I see it as an opportunity. Peer review has been under strain for years, and automated science forces us to finally rethink it: more transparency, more emphasis on reproducibility, maybe more continuous, open review rather than a single accept or reject. If we get that right, it benefits human-written science just as much as AI-generated science.

r001.rationale: The response says paper generation is becoming nearly free and that reviewers will face a flood of papers, shifting the bottleneck to evaluation.

r002.rationale: It mentions an automated reviewer and automated checks, but does not propose filtering papers so only the strongest advance to human verification.

r003.rationale: It discusses review and open review, but does not identify dissemination through the research community as part of ultimate verification.

r004.rationale: It calls for checking that code reproduces reported numbers and auditing experiments, which communicates running or reproducing experiments to verify findings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that an automated scientist is a machine for generating plausible-looking claims at scale, and peer review is the only mechanism we have whose job is to decide whether a plausible-looking claim is actually true. So the moment you remove the human bottleneck on the production side, you've just shifted all of the pressure onto the verification side.

When we built the AI Scientist, one of the things that struck me pretty early is that the system is very good at producing artifacts that have the shape of science. You get a hypothesis, you get an experiment, you get a paper with figures and related work and a nice abstract. And a lot of the time the content is reasonable. But some fraction of the time it's confidently wrong in ways that are quite subtle: the baseline wasn't tuned fairly, the metric got redefined halfway through, the experiment ran on a tiny budget and the conclusion is overclaimed. A human grad student makes those mistakes too, of course, but they make maybe one paper a year, and their advisor reads it. If you can generate a hundred papers overnight, nobody's advisor is reading all of those.

So there's a volume argument, and then there's a more interesting epistemic argument. Historically, the cost of writing a paper was itself a kind of filter. If somebody spent six months on something, that was at least weak evidence they believed in it. Automation destroys that signal. The paper no longer tells you anything about how much the author trusted the result, because there is no author in that sense. So the review has to carry all of the weight that effort and reputation used to carry.

And I'd actually go one step further. I think peer review has to change character, not just scale up. The traditional model is a reviewer reading a PDF and forming an opinion. For automated outputs, that's not sufficient, because the thing you most need to check is whether the experiment actually did what the text says it did. So you want reviewers, human or automated, who can rerun the code, inspect the logs, perturb the setup, check whether the result survives. Reproducibility stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the core of the review.

Which, somewhat ironically, is where automation can help again. We already found that an LLM reviewer can get roughly into the range of human agreement on certain conference papers. I don't think that means we replace human reviewers, but it means you can have a first-pass filter that catches the obviously broken stuff, and then the scarce human attention goes to the claims that are both surprising and seem to hold up. I think of it a bit like the relationship between a compiler and a code review. The compiler catches a whole class of errors cheaply, and then the human looks at whether the thing makes sense.

The failure mode I worry about is the opposite, where the community gets flooded, reviewers get exhausted, and the standard quietly drops because there's no way to keep up. Then you've lowered the bar exactly when you've raised the volume. So to me, if you're serious about automated science, you have to be at least as serious about automated and improved verification, otherwise you're just generating noise with better typesetting.

r001.rationale: It says automated scientists can generate a hundred papers overnight, shifting pressure onto reviewers and risking reviewer exhaustion.

r002.rationale: It proposes an LLM first-pass filter to catch broken papers, reserving scarce human attention for claims that appear surprising and robust.

r003.rationale: It discusses peer review and community overload but does not identify dissemination of findings through the research community as part of verification.

r004.rationale: It says reviewers should rerun code, inspect logs, and perturb the setup to check whether results hold.

astra-6.text:
I think automated scientists make peer review more important because they change the bottleneck. If you can generate hypotheses, run experiments, and write papers much faster, then producing a plausible scientific claim becomes relatively cheap. Establishing whether that claim is actually reliable still takes work.

You can imagine a system running thousands of experiments and finding something that looks compelling just by chance. The resulting paper might tell a very convincing story, but were the controls appropriate? Does the result hold up under different assumptions? Can somebody independently reproduce it? Those questions become more important as the volume of output increases.

And peer review itself will probably need automation to cope with that volume. But having another agent say, “Yes, this looks good,” isn't enough, especially if it shares the same blind spots as the system that produced the work. We need independent checks grounded in the experiments and the evidence. Otherwise, we're scaling the production of convincing papers without necessarily scaling scientific progress.

r001.rationale: It says automated systems can produce papers much faster and that the resulting volume makes peer review harder to handle, indicating increased reviewer workload.

r002.rationale: It discusses automating peer review but does not propose filtering papers so only the strongest advance to human verification.

r003.rationale: It mentions independent reproduction, but does not identify dissemination through the research community as part of ultimate verification.

r004.rationale: It refers to running experiments and checking evidence, but does not say verification of AI-generated research probably requires executing experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think automated scientists make peer review more important because they change the bottleneck. If we can generate hypotheses, run experiments, and write papers much faster, then producing a plausible scientific claim becomes cheap. Figuring out whether that claim is actually correct and meaningful becomes the hard part.

You can imagine a system producing a very polished paper where the experiments don’t really support the conclusion, or where there’s some subtle issue in the evaluation. Fluency doesn’t resolve any of that. You still need someone to ask: Is this the right experiment? Are the baselines fair? Can we reproduce the result? Does it actually teach us something?

And I think some of that review can itself be automated. But you want independent checks, rather than having the same system generate a claim and then congratulate itself for verifying it. So the opportunity is to scale scrutiny alongside discovery. Otherwise, we’ve just made it much easier to produce things that look like science.

r001.rationale: It says automated systems can produce claims and papers faster, but does not say this increases human reviewers’ workload.

r002.rationale: It mentions that some review could be automated, but does not propose filtering papers so only the strongest reach human reviewers.

r003.rationale: It discusses independent review and scrutiny, but not dissemination through the research community as part of verification.

r004.rationale: It asks whether experiments are appropriate and results reproducible, but does not suggest that verification probably requires executing experiments.
